profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized asset management firm between the Quant Research Lead and the Product Strategy Manager to prepare an internal pilot for a new 'sliding-window log-optimal portfolio' strategy inspired by a recent paper. The context is that the firm wants to decide how to package the strategy for a six-week internal evaluation before deciding whether to position it as a model-portfolio overlay for wealth advisors. The agenda is to define what the pilot will include, how performance will be summarized for the investment committee, what operations work is needed, who owns each deliverable, and the timeline for a 'Friday' planning checkpoint and a month-end review. The expected outcome is a shared plan for the pilot scope, presentation materials, operational setup, and responsibilities, while both participants leave believing they have aligned on the same implementation plan.

members.name: Nina Desai
members.expertise: systematic investing, portfolio construction, backtesting, and strategy prototyping
members.background: Nina has a PhD in financial engineering and leads the small quant research team that evaluates academic strategies for internal adoption; she regularly translates papers into research prototypes and hands cleaner versions to downstream teams.
members.private_state: Nina wants the pilot to demonstrate that the sliding-window method is materially better than the firm's current static Kelly-style benchmark, but she is also trying to minimize engineering overhead by keeping the exercise inside her team's existing research pipeline.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' for an internal strategy review mainly means a research-grade paper replication plus a concise committee deck, not a production-ready operating process.

When people say 'monthly rebalance' for a strategy prototype, they usually mean the weights are recalculated using data through the last trading day of the month and implemented at the next market open.

A 'window' in this context is the trailing estimation lookback used to re-estimate weights each rebalance date, and discussing a 36-month window does not require separately specifying overlap or data refresh mechanics.

If performance is said to be 'superior,' the natural standard in internal research is higher cumulative return over the test period with standard risk stats appended, not advisor-facing deliverability requirements.
Operations or compliance details for an internal evaluation are assumed to be light unless someone explicitly asks for live shadow-booking or advisor communication artifacts.

members.name: Owen Mercer
members.expertise: investment product packaging, governance processes, advisor rollout planning, and cross-functional launch coordination
members.background: Owen came from a multi-asset product team at a private bank and now turns research ideas into offerings that can pass investment committee review and fit the firm's advisor platform constraints.
members.private_state: Owen wants the pilot to look close enough to a launchable sleeve that the investment committee can quickly greenlight broader commercialization, and he is quietly concerned that quant research often hands over something elegant but operationally thin.
hidden_assumptions: An internal 'pilot' for the investment committee should resemble a near-launch package, including implementation assumptions, monitoring workflow, and enough documentation for downstream stakeholders.

When a team says 'monthly rebalance,' the practical meaning is trading during the standard month-end implementation cycle used by managed accounts, typically after month-end files are finalized rather than at next-day market open.

A 'window' discussion for a proposed product implicitly includes the client-facing review period over which the strategy will be judged in the pilot, not just the estimation lookback inside the model.

If a strategy is described as having 'superior performance,' that only really counts in committee terms if the result looks stable across model sleeves and can be communicated in the standard product scorecard format.

Any pilot expected to move forward should already assume some operational support steps such as implementation notes, exception handling, and a basic governance trail, even if not called out explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly agree to 'scope the pilot' and 'get the pilot ready for committee.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina understands the pilot as a research evaluation package: replicated results, internal backtest, benchmark comparison, and a short deck summarizing findings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Owen understands the pilot as a quasi-product package: research results plus implementation workflow, monitoring expectations, and enough operational documentation to support a committee go/no-go decision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to collaborative planning and the word 'pilot' sounds naturally shared; each assumes the other knows the firm's normal meaning from their own part of the organization, so neither sees a need to unpack the boundary explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the strategy will use a 'monthly rebalance' during the internal evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina assumes the model recomputes weights using data through the last trading day of each month and implements trades at the next market open in the research simulation and any shadow tracking.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Owen assumes the strategy follows the firm's managed-account implementation cycle, with trades executed in the regular month-end batch after holdings files and operational checks are finalized.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Monthly rebalance sounds like a settled operational convention rather than a controversial design choice; each interprets it through their own team's standard workflow and hears no obvious conflict in the other's wording.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on showing that the approach has 'superior performance' versus the current benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the pilot should demonstrate higher cumulative returns over the backtest and pilot shadow period, with supporting drawdown and turnover statistics included as context.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Owen means the strategy should look convincingly strong in the committee's standard scorecard, which implicitly requires consistency across subperiods and a presentation format comparable to existing model sleeves, not just stronger headline cumulative return.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same positive language and neither disputes the goal; because both standards often co-occur in polished materials, they each assume their preferred criterion is simply what 'superior' normally entails.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss using 'the 36-month window' in the plan.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina uses '36-month window' to mean the trailing estimation lookback used by the algorithm to recalculate log-optimal weights at each rebalance date.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Owen hears '36-month window' as the review horizon over which the pilot's results will be summarized for decision-makers, i.e., the three-year story they will present to committee.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In investment meetings, 'window' is common shorthand in both modeling and reporting contexts; because both are discussing planning rather than technical mechanics, the phrase feels fluent and neither participant suspects the other is anchoring on a different layer of the process.
